eras.summary: Grand Prix racing resumed with pre-war machinery and pre-war attitudes to risk. Fangio won five titles in eight seasons.
eras.defining_features: Front engines, drum brakes, no seatbelts, treaded road-style tyres, races of 500 km

eras.summary: Cooper put the engine behind the driver and the entire grid followed within three years. British 'garagiste' teams displaced the Italian manufacturers.
eras.defining_features: Mid-engined layout, monocoque chassis, the 1.5 L formula, the first Constructors' Championship

eras.era_name: The DFV and the birth of aerodynamics
eras.summary: The Cosworth DFV made independent constructors competitive; wings and then ground effect turned the car into an aerodynamic device. Fatality rates were at their worst.
eras.defining_features: 3.0 L formula, wings, sponsorship liveries, the beginning of the safety movement

eras.summary: Two revolutions at once: underbody downforce and forced induction. Power outputs reached figures never approached since.
eras.defining_features: Venturi tunnels, sliding skirts, 1,400 bhp qualifying engines, carbon-fibre chassis

eras.era_name: The electronic era and its aftermath
eras.summary: Active suspension, traction control and semi-automatic gearboxes arrived and were then banned. The 1994 accidents redefined the sport's relationship with risk.
eras.defining_features: Driver aids and their prohibition, the post-Imola safety programme, refuelling

eras.era_name: Ferrari's dominance and the manufacturer boom
eras.summary: Schumacher and Ferrari won five consecutive titles; car makers poured in money.
eras.defining_features: Grooved tyres, tyre wars, V10 then V8 engines, unlimited testing, escalating budgets

eras.summary: Rule packages designed to cut downforce were repeatedly outwitted — double diffusers, F-ducts, blown floors.
eras.defining_features: KERS, DRS, exhaust-blown diffusers, the arrival of Pirelli's degradation tyres

eras.summary: The most complex power units ever raced, and the longest period of single-team dominance in the sport's history.
eras.defining_features: 1.6 L V6 turbo hybrids, 50%+ thermal efficiency, eight consecutive Mercedes constructors' titles

eras.era_name: Ground effect returns and the cost cap bites
eras.summary: New aerodynamics intended to allow close following, alongside a budget cap that began to compress the field. Red Bull's 2023 was the most dominant season on record; by 2025 the top three drivers finished within thirteen points.
eras.defining_features: Venturi tunnels, porpoising, 18-inch wheels, the $135-145 m cost cap, sprint weekends

eras.summary: A smaller, lighter car, an even power split between combustion and electrical energy, sustainable fuel, and two new manufacturers.
eras.dominant_teams: TBD — Mercedes leads the opening half of 2026
eras.defining_features: Active aerodynamics, Overtake Mode, no MGU-H, 100% sustainable fuel, twelve teams

regulation_changes.title: World Championship established
regulation_changes.detail: The FIA created a Drivers' World Championship over six European Grands Prix plus the Indianapolis 500.
regulation_changes.impact: Turned a loose calendar of national Grands Prix into a single competition.

regulation_changes.title: Points to the top five plus fastest lap
regulation_changes.detail: 8-6-4-3-2 with one point for fastest lap, shared if tied. Only a driver's best four results counted.
regulation_changes.impact: Dropped scores would remain in some form until 1990.

regulation_changes.title: Championship run to Formula 2
regulation_changes.detail: 2.0 L naturally aspirated, adopted for 1952-53 after Alfa Romeo's withdrawal left too few competitive F1 cars.
regulation_changes.impact: Ascari won every race he entered across the two years.

regulation_changes.title: 2.5 L naturally aspirated formula
regulation_changes.detail: New capacity limit; supercharging limited to 750 cc and effectively abandoned.
regulation_changes.impact: Drew Mercedes and Lancia into the championship.

regulation_changes.title: International Cup for F1 Manufacturers
regulation_changes.detail: The first Constructors' Championship, awarded to Vanwall.
regulation_changes.impact: Made the constructor, not just the driver, a championship competitor.

regulation_changes.title: Commercial fuel mandated
regulation_changes.detail: Avgas replaced exotic alcohol fuel blends; race distances cut from 500 km to 300 km.
regulation_changes.impact: Cut power and cost, and shortened races to roughly two hours.

regulation_changes.title: 1.5 L formula
regulation_changes.detail: Capacity halved and a minimum weight of 450 kg imposed.
regulation_changes.impact: Fiercely opposed by British teams, who were unprepared; Ferrari dominated 1961.

regulation_changes.title: 3.0 L formula
regulation_changes.detail: Capacity doubled, or 1.5 L with forced induction.
regulation_changes.impact: 'The return of power'; the Cosworth DFV followed in 1967.

regulation_changes.title: Commercial sponsorship permitted
regulation_changes.detail: The FIA allowed liveries other than national racing colours.
regulation_changes.impact: Gold Leaf Team Lotus appeared in red, white and gold. The sport's commercial model begins here.

regulation_changes.title: High wings banned mid-season
regulation_changes.detail: Following strut failures for both Lotus drivers at Barcelona, tall aerofoils on unsprung mountings were outlawed.
regulation_changes.impact: Aerodynamic devices were henceforth required to be fixed to the sprung mass and limited in height.

regulation_changes.title: Mandatory deformable structure and fuel bag tanks
regulation_changes.detail: Crushable structures around fuel cells and self-sealing bag tanks required.
regulation_changes.impact: Directly reduced fire deaths, the era's dominant killer.

regulation_changes.title: Airbox regulations and safety structures
regulation_changes.detail: Rollover bar dimensions specified; onboard fire extinguishers and electrical cut-off required.

regulation_changes.title: Deformable structures around the cockpit
regulation_changes.detail: Side crash structures mandated.

regulation_changes.title: Tall airboxes banned
regulation_changes.detail: Mid-season ban following the airbox height arms race.

regulation_changes.title: First turbocharged car
regulation_changes.detail: Renault exploited the long-dormant 1.5 L forced-induction option with the RS01.
regulation_changes.impact: Began an eleven-year turbo arms race.

regulation_changes.title: First Concorde Agreement
regulation_changes.detail: Settled the FISA-FOCA war over commercial rights and rule-making between the governing body, the teams and the commercial rights holder.
regulation_changes.impact: Established the tripartite governance model that still applies.

regulation_changes.title: Sliding skirts banned; 6 cm ride height minimum
regulation_changes.detail: Aimed at killing ground effect.
regulation_changes.impact: Circumvented by hydropneumatic suspension that lowered the car at speed.

regulation_changes.title: Flat bottoms mandated
regulation_changes.detail: Underbody had to be flat between the axles, ending Venturi tunnels.
regulation_changes.impact: Cornering speeds fell sharply; downforce moved back to wings.

regulation_changes.title: Refuelling banned; 220 litre fuel limit
regulation_changes.detail: Race fuel capped to restrain turbo power.
regulation_changes.impact: Turbo engines were detuned for races and unleashed in qualifying.

regulation_changes.title: Naturally aspirated engines outlawed
regulation_changes.detail: Turbo-only season, the sole one in the sport's history.

regulation_changes.title: 4.0 bar boost limit; naturally aspirated cars readmitted
regulation_changes.detail: 3.5 L atmospheric engines permitted alongside boost-limited turbos, with separate trophies.
regulation_changes.impact: Began the managed phase-out of turbos.

regulation_changes.title: 2.5 bar boost limit and 150 litre fuel limit
regulation_changes.detail: Final year of turbo eligibility.
regulation_changes.impact: McLaren-Honda still won 15 of 16 races.

regulation_changes.title: Turbocharging banned
regulation_changes.detail: 3.5 L naturally aspirated only.
regulation_changes.impact: Ended the highest-power era in the sport's history.

regulation_changes.title: Dropped scores abolished
regulation_changes.detail: All results counted towards the championship for the first time.
regulation_changes.impact: Simplified the championship and ended the era of gross-versus-net point totals.

regulation_changes.title: Emergency in-season rule changes
regulation_changes.detail: After Imola: plank under the floor, reduced airbox and diffuser, larger cockpit opening, restricted front wing endplates.
regulation_changes.impact: The most abrupt safety intervention in the sport's history.

regulation_changes.title: Refuelling reintroduced
regulation_changes.detail: Mid-race refuelling permitted from 1994.
regulation_changes.impact: Made race strategy a central competitive variable for sixteen years.

regulation_changes.title: Electronic driver aids banned
regulation_changes.detail: Active suspension, traction control, ABS, four-wheel steering and launch control outlawed.
regulation_changes.impact: Cars became markedly harder to drive; the enforcement difficulty led to traction control being legalised again in 2001.

regulation_changes.title: 3.0 L capacity limit
regulation_changes.detail: Engine capacity cut from 3.5 L.
regulation_changes.impact: A direct response to the 1994 accidents.

regulation_changes.title: Higher cockpit sides mandated
regulation_changes.detail: Head protection raised around the cockpit rim.

regulation_changes.title: Narrow-track cars and grooved tyres
regulation_changes.detail: Track cut from 2.0 m to 1.8 m; three grooves front and four rear.
regulation_changes.impact: Cut cornering speed at the expense of mechanical grip.

regulation_changes.title: Traction control legalised
regulation_changes.detail: Reinstated from the Spanish GP because the ban had become unpoliceable.
regulation_changes.impact: Banned again in 2008 with the standard ECU.

regulation_changes.title: Points to the top eight; single-lap qualifying
regulation_changes.detail: 10-8-6-5-4-3-2-1 introduced; parc ferme rules restricted set-up changes after qualifying.
regulation_changes.impact: Deliberately designed to reduce Ferrari's margin.

regulation_changes.title: Team orders banned
regulation_changes.detail: Following the 2002 Austrian GP, orders that interfere with a race result were prohibited.
regulation_changes.impact: Repealed in 2011 as unenforceable.

regulation_changes.title: One engine per two race weekends; tyre changes banned
regulation_changes.detail: Engines had to last two events; tyres could not be changed during a race.
regulation_changes.impact: The tyre rule was abandoned after the 2005 US GP fiasco.

regulation_changes.title: 2.4 L V8 engines
regulation_changes.detail: V10s replaced to cut power and cost.

regulation_changes.title: Single tyre supplier
regulation_changes.detail: Bridgestone became the sole supplier after Michelin's withdrawal.
regulation_changes.impact: Ended tyre-war development and made tyres a controlled variable.

regulation_changes.title: Standard ECU
regulation_changes.detail: A single McLaren Electronic Systems ECU for all cars.
regulation_changes.impact: Made traction control and engine braking control enforceable to ban.

regulation_changes.title: Aerodynamic overhaul and KERS
regulation_changes.detail: Wide low front wing, narrow high rear wing, most bodywork appendages removed; optional 60 kW kinetic energy recovery.
regulation_changes.impact: First serious attempt to design for following another car. The double-diffuser loophole dominated the season.

regulation_changes.title: Refuelling banned; new points system
regulation_changes.detail: Race refuelling prohibited; 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1 introduced with the field expanded to 24 cars.
regulation_changes.impact: Fuel loads at the start became a major performance factor.

regulation_changes.title: DRS and Pirelli high-degradation tyres
regulation_changes.detail: A driver-adjustable rear wing usable within one second of the car ahead in designated zones, and tyres designed to fall off deliberately.
regulation_changes.impact: Both were explicit attempts to manufacture overtaking; both remain contested on sporting-purity grounds.

regulation_changes.title: Double points at the finale
regulation_changes.detail: The last race awarded double points.
regulation_changes.impact: Used once, universally disliked, and dropped.

regulation_changes.title: 1.6 L V6 turbo-hybrid power units
regulation_changes.detail: ERS with MGU-K and MGU-H, 100 kg fuel limit and 100 kg/h flow limit; five power-unit elements per season.
regulation_changes.impact: The most radical technical change in the sport's history. Thermal efficiency passed 50%. Development costs pushed several independent engine builders out.

regulation_changes.title: Virtual Safety Car
regulation_changes.detail: A field-wide delta-time speed restriction introduced after Jules Bianchi's accident at Suzuka.
regulation_changes.impact: Allows yellow-flag conditions to be enforced without bunching the field.

regulation_changes.title: Wider cars and tyres
regulation_changes.detail: Cars widened to 2.0 m, wider tyres, larger diffuser and lower rear wing.
regulation_changes.impact: Lap records fell across the calendar; following became harder.

regulation_changes.title: Halo mandated
regulation_changes.detail: A titanium cockpit protection structure able to withstand 12 tonnes.
regulation_changes.impact: Initially unpopular on aesthetic grounds; credited with saving Leclerc at Spa 2018, Grosjean at Bahrain 2020 and Zhou at Silverstone 2022.

regulation_changes.title: Point for fastest lap
regulation_changes.detail: One point for the fastest lap, if finishing in the top ten.
regulation_changes.impact: Removed again from 2025.

regulation_changes.title: Cost cap introduced
regulation_changes.detail: A budget cap of $145 m for 2021, excluding driver salaries, marketing and the three highest-paid staff.
regulation_changes.impact: The most consequential governance change since the Concorde Agreement; designed to compress the competitive order.

regulation_changes.title: Sprint format trialled
regulation_changes.detail: Three events ran a short Saturday race setting the grid, with points to the top three.
regulation_changes.impact: Extended to six events; sprint results decoupled from the Grand Prix grid from 2024.

regulation_changes.title: Ground effect returns
regulation_changes.detail: Venturi tunnels reinstated with simplified over-body aerodynamics, 18-inch wheels and standardised parts.
regulation_changes.impact: Intended to let cars follow closely. Porpoising — aerodynamic bouncing — dominated the first season and forced a mid-2022 technical directive on floor stiffness and a vertical-oscillation metric.

regulation_changes.title: Floor edge and stiffness rules tightened
regulation_changes.detail: Floor edges raised and diffuser throat height increased to curb porpoising.

regulation_changes.title: Fastest lap point removed
regulation_changes.detail: The bonus point introduced in 2019 was dropped.
regulation_changes.impact: Removed an incentive for late 'free' pit stops by out-of-contention cars.

regulation_changes.title: Tougher homologation tests
regulation_changes.detail: Roll-hoop vertical impact requirement raised from 16 g to 20 g; a two-stage nose-cone concept introduced.

regulation_changes.title: Overtake Mode
regulation_changes.detail: A driver within one second at the detection point receives additional energy deployment — the FIA/F1 overview describes an extra 0.5 MJ and a raised deployment profile.
regulation_changes.impact: The successor mechanism to DRS's overtaking assistance.

regulation_changes.title: New chassis formula
regulation_changes.detail: Wheelbase capped at 3,400 mm, width reduced to 1,900 mm, minimum weight 768 kg (722 kg car and driver plus 46 kg estimated tyre mass in the FIA overview).
regulation_changes.impact: The first deliberate reduction in car size and weight in decades.

regulation_changes.title: Active aerodynamics replace DRS
regulation_changes.detail: Driver-operable front and rear wing systems with distinct low-drag and high-downforce modes.
regulation_changes.impact: Removes the DRS proximity mechanism in favour of a mode both cars can use.

regulation_changes.title: MGU-H removed
regulation_changes.detail: The turbo-driven heat-energy recovery unit is deleted from the power unit.
regulation_changes.impact: Cut cost and complexity; explicitly credited with attracting Audi, Ford and General Motors.

regulation_changes.title: Roughly 50/50 power split
regulation_changes.detail: Electrical output raised to approximately 350 kW, against a comparable figure from the internal combustion engine.

regulation_changes.title: 100% advanced sustainable fuel
regulation_changes.detail: Fully sustainable drop-in fuel mandated.
regulation_changes.impact: The sport's principal decarbonisation claim for the ruleset.

technical_innovations.description: Cooper's rear-engined 500 cc cars scaled up to Grand Prix racing by 1958-59.
technical_innovations.legacy: Universal from 1961; every F1 car since has had the engine behind the driver.

technical_innovations.description: Positively closed valves and direct fuel injection derived from aero-engine work.
technical_innovations.legacy: Injection became universal; desmodromics did not.

technical_innovations.description: A stressed-skin aluminium tub replacing the spaceframe.
technical_innovations.legacy: Halved chassis weight and roughly trebled torsional stiffness. Now universal, in carbon fibre.

technical_innovations.innovation: The Cosworth DFV as a stressed member
technical_innovations.description: The engine bolted directly to the rear of the monocoque and carried the suspension loads.
technical_innovations.legacy: Made the small independent constructor viable for two decades.

technical_innovations.description: Inverted aerofoils generating downforce.
technical_innovations.legacy: The single most important performance concept in the sport's history.

technical_innovations.description: Radiators moved from the nose to the flanks, giving a wedge profile and cleaner front-end airflow.
technical_innovations.legacy: Standard layout ever since.

technical_innovations.description: Four small front wheels to cut frontal area while retaining braking and grip.
technical_innovations.legacy: Won the 1976 Swedish GP. Tyre development killed it; four-wheel cars mandated from 1983.

technical_innovations.description: Inverted-wing underbody profiles with sliding skirts sealing the low-pressure area.
technical_innovations.legacy: Transformed cornering speed. Banned in 1983, reintroduced in modified form in 2022.

technical_innovations.description: 1.5 L forced-induction engine exploiting a long-ignored rule.
technical_innovations.legacy: Defined 1980s F1 and produced the highest power figures ever seen in the sport.

technical_innovations.description: A fan, nominally for cooling, extracting air from beneath the car to generate suction.
technical_innovations.legacy: Won its only race, the 1978 Swedish GP, and was withdrawn under pressure.

technical_innovations.description: The first F1 chassis made from carbon composite.
technical_innovations.legacy: Vastly stronger and lighter than aluminium; the foundation of modern survival-cell safety. Universal within four years.

technical_innovations.description: Electrohydraulic paddle-shift with no clutch pedal for upshifts.
technical_innovations.legacy: Universal by the mid-1990s.

technical_innovations.description: Computer-controlled hydraulic ride height maintaining optimum aerodynamic platform.
technical_innovations.legacy: Devastatingly effective; banned for 1994.

technical_innovations.description: A second brake pedal acting on one rear wheel to rotate the car.
technical_innovations.legacy: Banned once revealed, as a four-wheel-steering device.

technical_innovations.description: A sprung mass in the nose damping tyre oscillation and stabilising the aerodynamic platform.
technical_innovations.legacy: Banned mid-2006 as a movable aerodynamic device.

technical_innovations.description: Front wishbone mounting philosophies to clean up airflow under the nose.
technical_innovations.legacy: Superseded by pull-rod and high-nose concepts.

technical_innovations.description: A second-tier diffuser exploiting a gap in the wording of the 2009 rules.
technical_innovations.legacy: Effectively decided the 2009 championship; banned for 2011.

technical_innovations.description: 60 kW kinetic energy recovery under braking.
technical_innovations.legacy: The bridgehead to the hybrid era.

technical_innovations.description: A driver-operated duct stalling the rear wing on the straights for less drag.
technical_innovations.legacy: Banned for 2011 as a movable aerodynamic device operated by the driver.

technical_innovations.description: Exhaust gases routed into the diffuser to energise it, including off-throttle.
technical_innovations.legacy: Progressively restricted 2011-2013 through exhaust position rules.

technical_innovations.description: Driver-adjustable rear wing within one second of the car ahead.
technical_innovations.legacy: Replaced by active aerodynamics and Overtake Mode in 2026.

technical_innovations.description: Compressor at the front of the engine and turbine at the rear, joined by a shaft through the vee, with the MGU-H between them.
technical_innovations.legacy: Gave Mercedes a package advantage that took rivals several seasons to answer.

technical_innovations.description: A small pre-combustion chamber igniting an ultra-lean main charge.
technical_innovations.legacy: Took thermal efficiency past 50%, roughly double a typical road petrol engine.

technical_innovations.description: Elaborate flow-conditioning structures ahead of the sidepods.
technical_innovations.legacy: Largely legislated away for 2022 to reduce wake sensitivity.

technical_innovations.description: Pushing and pulling the steering column altered front wheel toe on the move.
technical_innovations.legacy: Legal in 2020, explicitly banned for 2021.

technical_innovations.description: A radical narrow-sidepod interpretation of the ground-effect rules.
technical_innovations.legacy: Abandoned after two seasons; a rare example of a distinctive concept that simply did not work.

safety_milestones.milestone: Fuel and crowd control questions raised
safety_milestones.trigger_event: Von Trips's Monza crash killing 15 spectators
safety_milestones.description: Spectator placement began to be treated as a design problem rather than a local matter.
Jackie Stewart's campaign for barriers, run-off, medical facilities and marshalling standards begins in earnest.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Multiple fatalities including Clark, Spence, Schlesser and Bandini
safety_milestones.description: Rollover protection specified; full-face helmets adopted.

safety_milestones.milestone: Bag fuel tanks and deformable structures
safety_milestones.description: Self-sealing fuel cells became mandatory.
Standardised restraint and fire suppression.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Roger Williamson's death in a fire at Zandvoort with no marshal intervention
safety_milestones.description: Marshalling and fire-crew standards overhauled alongside the car rules.

safety_milestones.milestone: Permanent medical car and travelling medical delegate
safety_milestones.description: Professor Sid Watkins appointed in 1978; a doctor now travels with the championship.

safety_milestones.milestone: Standardised race-start procedure and medical helicopter
safety_milestones.trigger_event: Ronnie Peterson's death after a delayed extraction at Monza
safety_milestones.description: A helicopter capable of flying must be on site or the race does not start.
Minimum crash structure ahead of the driver's feet.
Cars had to pass a static and then dynamic impact test to be eligible.

safety_milestones.milestone: Driver's feet behind the front axle line
safety_milestones.description: Ended the practice of pedals ahead of the front wheels.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Deaths of Senna and Ratzenberger, injuries to Wendlinger, Barrichello and Lehto
safety_milestones.description: Immediate aerodynamic cuts, then a multi-year programme: higher cockpit sides, larger cockpit template, wheel tethers, stronger side impact structures, and the FIA Institute's crash-research programme.
Head and neck protection around the cockpit rim.
Tethers to retain wheels; strengthened repeatedly since, with double tethers from 2011.

safety_milestones.milestone: Higher cockpit sides and headrest energy absorption

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Basilar skull fractures in motorsport worldwide
safety_milestones.description: Head and neck support tethering the helmet to the shoulders; the single most effective driver-protection device of its generation.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Felipe Massa struck by a loose spring at the Hungaroring; Henry Surtees killed in F2
safety_milestones.description: A ballistic strip added to helmet visors.

safety_milestones.milestone: Virtual Safety Car and closed pit-lane research
safety_milestones.description: VSC introduced for 2015; the accident also began the closed-cockpit research programme.
Recovery vehicles may not be on track without VSC or safety car.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Bianchi's death and the Justin Wilson and Henry Surtees fatalities in other categories
safety_milestones.description: A titanium structure withstanding 12 tonnes, roughly the weight of a London bus. Credited with saving lives at Spa 2018, Bahrain 2020 and Silverstone 2022.

safety_milestones.milestone: Stronger chassis and higher-load survival cell
safety_milestones.description: Front and side impact loads increased substantially.
Preceded further increases after Zhou Guanyu's 2022 Silverstone crash, in which the roll hoop failed.

safety_milestones.trigger_event: Zhou Guanyu's inverted crash at Silverstone
safety_milestones.description: Roll-hoop homologation revised to eliminate pointed designs that could dig into the surface.

safety_milestones.milestone: Roll-hoop vertical test raised to 20 g
safety_milestones.description: Up from 16 g, alongside a two-stage nose-cone concept in the 2026 framework.

tyre_suppliers.notes: Belgian supplier, closely associated with Ferrari.
Present at Indianapolis from the start and in Grand Prix racing from 1966.

known_gaps.description: race_entries holds the winner, the pole-sitter and the fastest-lap setter for every race - about 2.1 rows per race against a real field of 15 to 22. Second place, third place, retirements, grid positions and per-race points are NOT in the distributed database. They are available: 26,137 rows covering 1950-2026 sit behind the Jolpica-F1 API, and tools/ergast_load.py fetches and loads them, self-validating on the winner already stored. It is not part of the build because the build is offline. Until it is run, drivers.podiums stays hand-entered for the 7 drivers who have an official figure and is NULL for everyone else, and 73 register entries have no race rows at all.
known_gaps.resolution: python3 tools/ergast_load.py  (about 270 requests, a few minutes). Then rerun verify.py: the podium reconciliation compares the derived counts against the official figures and is what proves the load. Do NOT transcribe these rows by hand - an attempt to do so during v2.7 put fabricated results into four of five sampled 2008 rows, and only that reconciliation caught it.

known_gaps.area: the car each race was won in
known_gaps.description: 29 cars are in the register, all of them landmarks, with full specifications and a design history. They are linked to races through data/cars.py CAR_SEASONS, which asserts per (car, season) that a constructor ran one chassis that year. That covers 262 of 2,424 race entries. It stops where a team ran two cars in a season - Lotus in 1970, Cooper in 1960, Williams in 1982 - because a blanket year link would then be wrong, and it stops entirely for the several hundred chassis that never won anything. The register is deliberately not a list of every car that ever started a Grand Prix.
known_gaps.resolution: Harvest the chassis model per race from the season articles, which print it in the same results table the winners came from. Reject any value the article does not actually contain: a trial harvest of 1952 returned an inferred 'Ferrari 125 F2' for races Ascari won in a Ferrari 500, and the winner cross-check does not catch that, so the harvested chassis must also be checked against that season's entry list before it is stored.

known_gaps.area: the car each pole was taken in
known_gaps.description: The pole and fastest-lap harvest recorded who set them but not what they drove, so 655 of 1,161 pole entries carry no constructor and cannot be linked to a car. A car's derived pole count is therefore a lower bound, and verify.py only checks that it does not EXCEED the published figure. Derived win counts have no such problem and match the published totals exactly for all 11 fully linked cars.
known_gaps.resolution: Harvest the constructor alongside the pole-sitter, or infer it from the driver's entry that season once season_entries covers the historical seasons.

known_gaps.area: lap times, tyre stints, pit stops, radio and telemetry
known_gaps.description: Formula 1 publishes per-lap timing only from 2018, through the live timing API. The laps, stints, pit_stops, race_control_messages and team_radio tables exist and are empty in the distributed database because this build environment has no network access to that API. tools/fastf1_load.py fills them - see ./f1 telemetry. Car telemetry itself (speed, throttle, brake, gear at about 4 Hz) is deliberately NOT stored here: it is hundreds of megabytes per weekend and the loader writes it to Parquet beside the database instead. There is no lap-by-lap data of any kind before 2018 and there is no prospect of any: it was never recorded in a retrievable form.
known_gaps.resolution: pip install fastf1, then python3 tools/fastf1_load.py --years 2018-2026 --results --radio. That also fills the full classified finishing order for those seasons, checked against the winner already stored.

known_gaps.area: pole, fastest lap and race times per race
known_gaps.description: The race_timing table is empty. These figures are published per race rather than per season, so filling them for 1950-2017 means reading 1,161 individual race articles, which was judged too expensive against what it returns. From 2018 the FastF1 loader supplies the same information at far greater resolution.
known_gaps.resolution: Either harvest race articles for the pre-2018 seasons, or accept that timing starts in 2018 and fill it with tools/fastf1_load.py.

known_gaps.area: circuit configuration as raced, for most circuits
known_gaps.description: Thirteen circuits have a complete configuration timeline: Spa, Monza, Silverstone, Hockenheim, Interlagos, Indianapolis, Catalunya, Albert Park, the Spielberg site, the Mexico City site, Bahrain, Marina Bay and Yas Marina. For every other circuit the database holds one set of figures - the most recent - so a 1976 Kyalami lap is reported at the length of the 1992 rebuild. v_race_venues is explicit about this: its 'figures' column reads 'as raced' where a layout row covers the year and 'current layout' where it does not. Zandvoort, Suzuka, Imola, Jerez, Estoril, Paul Ricard, Zolder, Brands Hatch, Kyalami and Buenos Aires all changed shape between championship races and are not yet broken out.
known_gaps.resolution: Research the configuration history of each remaining multi-race circuit and add the rows; verify.py already enforces that a circuit's layout rows, once present, form a complete non-overlapping timeline.

known_gaps.description: No fastest lap is recorded because none was set. The race was abandoned after two laps behind the safety car, half points were awarded and no racing lap was completed. This is a true null, not missing data.
